issues.issue: The voting requirements may be "waived by mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused", while Section 19.6.c allows the Accused and Accuser alone to agree to proceed without the minimum composition. The two waiver mechanisms require different consents.

"Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" is missing its verb ("are"), a slip that leaves the sentence incomplete. The defect is grammatical rather than substantive.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents", a standard with no ascertainable content. It cannot be applied without construction.

This section says the UAB "shall hear appeals of decisions of ... the Special Examiner's Process", but the Section 22.6 Appeals Procedures provide that the UAB only reads written submissions and reports its opinions to the Dean, who retains the discretion to amend or uphold his own decision. The two descriptions of the appellate function conflict.

The UAB is to have "one faculty Chairperson" appointed by the Dean, yet the composition sentence also gives it "two members of the faculty" as voting members while Section 20.7 says an Associate Dean "will serve as Chairperson". The provision does not state whether the Chairperson votes except to break ties.

Section 20.7 provides that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as Chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while this section requires a Chairperson "who is a full-time tenured faculty member" appointed by the Dean. The two cannot both be satisfied.

The factors the decision-maker "may consider" are expressly "including but not limited to", so the enumerated considerations do not confine the discretion at all. "Whenever appropriate" leaves the learning component equally open.

"Sanctions shall not take effect until approved by" the named administrators cannot be reconciled with the Special Examiner's Process, which provides that "[a]ny and all sanctions, including suspension or dismissal, will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". The instrument states two contradictory rules on when sanctions bite.
"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" attaches unspecified obligations to what is described as a warning. What may be imposed under a "warning" is undefined.

The privileges that may be lost are "including, but not limited to" a list of specific campus privileges, so the sanction's outer limit is undefined. Whether it could reach academic participation is left open.

A student on probation is subject to further discipline if they "in any way fail to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community", a condition with no ascertainable boundary. It is broader than any enumerated code violation.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is garbled — words are evidently missing after "until". The duration and consequences of a suspension cannot be read from it.

"The University may take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable under the circumstances" on mere "reason to believe" that conduct "may disrupt" safety or well-being confers a power bounded only by the University's own belief. Both the trigger and the permitted response are open-ended.

This unlimited power to alter a student's status is difficult to square with Section 22.2, which provides that pending final action a student's status "shall not be altered" except for reasons of "imminent danger".

The "imminent danger" precondition for altering a student's status pending final action conflicts with Sections 2.1.f and 3.0, which permit emergency suspension of any student merely accused or involved in an incident, and with Section 22.1's power to take "any action" on reason to believe conduct "may disrupt" well-being.

Indefinite suspension may follow a student being merely "charged with" a crime, and the Dean "must consider the nature of the crime and the risk" without any stated standard for the outcome. The provision confers a power whose limits are not stated.

The statement that "[t]he procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" cannot be squared with Section 22.2, which requires the Section 19.1 procedures to be implemented within 10 class days of any separation from campus.

Off-campus behaviour is sanctionable if "in the judgment of the Dean" it is inconsistent with being a "good citizen and good neighbor" and "adversely affects the University community". These are standards of pure discretion whose content is not fixed by the text.

Excluding the Section 19 procedural standards from "off-campus behavior or Dean's Sanctions" leaves dismissal available with no hearing, which is in tension with Section 18.0's statement that disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS".

The protocol is triggered by "severe emotional or psychological distress" and bars all campus access with "no exception for examinations", yet the section also gives the Dean discretion to "reinstate or restore" privileges. The criteria for either step are unstated.

The promise that "Brandeis is committed to acknowledging and preserving the rights and responsibilities of all its students through all of its disciplinary procedures" sits against a process that withholds the rights guaranteed by Section 19.10.C — an Advisor's active help, presenting and questioning witnesses, a hearing. Whether the commitment is operative or hortatory is a genuine question.

The definition permits an attorney to hold the Advisor role "when co-existing criminal proceedings exist", but simultaneously says the Advisor's role "is passive, and does not include writing or speaking on behalf of their party". What the attorney-Advisor may actually do is left unclear.

Section 19.6.d forbids a party to "employ professional legal counsel or other persons from outside the University community" to advise during a hearing, and the Section 3 services list describes counsel as limited to "passive assistance". This definition instead lets the attorney occupy the Advisor role outright.

The Director decides "in conjunction with the Dean of Student Life" which process applies, whereas Section 22.6 says that a case goes to the Special Examiner's Process whenever "the DSRCS receives a report and determines" a possible Section 3 or 7 violation exists. Whether the routing is discretionary or automatic is unresolved.

The definition does not state who appoints the Special Examiner, what qualifications or independence are required, or whether the Examiner may find facts as opposed to summarising them. The role is described only by what it produces.

The Observer must be "currently or formerly a member of the Student Conduct Board or formerly of the University Appeals Board" — an unexplained asymmetry that excludes sitting UAB members without saying so directly. The eligibility rule reads as a drafting slip.

This definition covers a person with "direct knowledge of the incident", whereas Section 19.6.e defines witnesses as those with "information directly related to the incident in question". The two definitions of the same term do not match.

Making the Dean the renderer of the "Final Decision" is hard to square with Section 20.7, under which the UAB "shall hear appeals of decisions of ... the Special Examiner's Process": the Dean reviews the appeal from his own decision.

Confining the UAB to "a report of its opinions to the Dean of Student Life" contradicts Section 19.7, under which a meritorious appeal requires the UAB to "conduct a new hearing" and permits it to reverse or alter the sanction, and Section 20.7's grant of appellate jurisdiction.

This process applies a "preponderance of the evidence" standard, while Section 19.6.i permits a finding of responsibility for the same code of conduct "based only upon clear and convincing evidence". The instrument sets two different standards of proof.

The 60-day period is framed as a "goal" to be met "or as soon as is practicable if unusual circumstances exist", so whether it is an enforceable commitment or an aspiration is genuinely contestable. "Without unnecessary delay" adds no measurable content.

A failure to cooperate lets the Special Examiner "consider the Accused to have accepted responsibility", and the phase is described as "the principal opportunity" to submit information — neither term is defined, and the deemed admission has no stated threshold. The provision is drafted one-sidedly against the Accused.

The statement that the process "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused" conflicts with Section 18.0, which limits discipline to persons "enrolled in any academic program", and with the Note to Section 19.1 permitting deferral when a student is withdrawn.

Evidence "deemed by the Special Examiner to be of material importance" is to be "shared equally with the parties", but the Examiner "retains the discretion not to share certain records". The two sentences leave the parties' access to the record undetermined.
This limited disclosure cannot be squared with Section 19.6.g, which gives the Accused and the Accuser "the right to view and question all evidence and reports presented" to the decision-maker.
Whether any witness is interviewed at all rests wholly on "the discretion of the Special Examiner", with no criterion stated. The sentence also contains the duplicated words "with the the parties".

Section 19.10.C.2 states a party's right "[t]o present witnesses on their own behalf", whereas this provision leaves who is interviewed entirely to the Examiner. The two allocations of control over witnesses differ.

Conducting the parties' interviews "separately" with no opportunity to question the other party cannot be reconciled with the right "[t]o question witnesses appearing against them" stated in Section 19.10.C.3 and Section 19.6.g.
The Examiner need only make "a good-faith effort to contact all pertinent witnesses", and "pertinent" is left to the Examiner's own judgment. The obligation cannot be measured.

The report "summarizes undisputed and disputed facts, and may offer conclusions or recommendations as to the credibility of testimony or potential outcomes" — whether the Examiner may find facts and credibility, or only summarise, is left permissive and unresolved. The Examiner's function is stated in the alternative.

The Dean decides on findings made by another person after separate meetings with each party, which cannot be reconciled with Section 19.6.i's rule that decisions "shall be based solely upon evidence and testimony introduced at the hearing" in the presence of both parties.

The Dean is to render the Final Decision "no earlier than 4 business days, and usually within 7 business days", a mix of a hard floor and a soft ceiling. "Usually" leaves the outer limit unenforceable.

Describing the Dean's decision as "the binding Final Decision" is in tension with the appeal rights in the Section 22.6 Appeals Procedures and in Section 20.7, under which the decision remains subject to review.

Withdrawal of the allegation "will terminate the Special Examiner's Process", yet the University "reserves the right to take actions against the Accused outside of" it, without identifying what actions or under what procedure. The reservation swallows the termination.

An acceptance of responsibility is made "non-reversible" with no provision for withdrawal on grounds of mistake or coercion, and no statement of what disclosure the Accused has had at that point. The finality term is absolute on its face.

The decision is delivered "within 7 days under usual circumstances" and the finding will be "announced" with supporting information merely "referenced", not disclosed. What the Accused is entitled to receive is left indefinite.

Sanctions are those "deemed appropriate by the Dean", whereas Section 21.1 provides that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved by" the Director or a Dean and Section 21.0 frames sanctioning as the province of the DSRCS administrator, the SCB or the UAB. The allocation of sanctioning authority differs between the two sections.

Appeals lie "only" on four grounds, one of which — "denial of rights under this process" — is open-ended, so the closed list is undermined by its own catch-all. What rights exist "under this process" is nowhere enumerated.

The UAB here merely submits "a written report ... of their opinions, thoughts, and suggestions" to the Dean, who "will retain the discretion to amend or uphold the original Final Decision", which contradicts Section 20.7 (the UAB "shall hear appeals") and Section 19.7 (a meritorious appeal produces "a new hearing" with power to reverse or alter the sanction).
